WHY TRADITIONAL CAREER "PLAYBOOKS" ARE OBSOLETE IN THE AGE OF AI

Entry-level corporate jobs are disappearing and the traditional career ladder is changing with them.

For decades, the standard formula for career success was straightforward: earn a degree, land an entry-level role, and spend your first few years doing routine work debugging basic code, reviewing standard contracts, or drafting routine copy. That repetitive work wasn't just busywork; it was the apprenticeship that built the judgment needed for senior roles.
Today, AI executes those foundational "playbook" tasks in seconds. As Palantir CEO Alex Karp recently pointed out, if your education only trained you to follow established frameworks, you are competing directly with software.

So, who actually holds long-term career leverage in the age of AI? According to Karp, it comes down to two distinct groups whose work cannot be reduced to a set of instructions:

1. SKILLED TRADESPEOPLE: ELECTRICIANS, PLUMBERS, CARPENTERS, and WELDERS operate in unpredictable physical environments. While AI excels at abstract logic, physical perception and on-site judgment remain extraordinarily difficult to automate. When a pipe bursts in an old building with no blueprints, software can't fix it experienced human hands and senses do.

2. NEURODIVERGENT THINKERS: Individuals with dyslexia, ADHD, or autism often struggle with rigid, linear "playbooks." Instead, they learn to see problems holistically, connect unexpected dots, and spot anomalies that standard processes smooth over. What traditional hiring once viewed as friction is rapidly becoming a core competitive advantage.

Palantir is already acting on this shift launching fellowships that bypass college degrees entirely and actively recruiting neurodivergent builders for their unique problem-solving strengths.

As AI handles the routine execution, human value shifts toward physical mastery and unconventional thinking.
How is AI changing entry-level hiring and skill development in your industry?

#FutureOfWork #AI #CareerDevelopment #HiringTrends #Leadership

​A clean verification check only proves that an AI followed its instructions. It does not prove those instructions were right.

​That distinction is happening right now with the proposed AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. Independent checks confirmed that the 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a verification language that checks logical steps, compile without internal errors. Yet the mathematics community has not declared the problem solved.

​Mathematicians are now doing a different kind of audit. They are checking the premises.
​Specifically, they are inspecting the starting rules and formal definitions entered into Lean at the beginning. If a definition quietly alters the original math problem, or if a hidden assumption slipped into the setup, the compiler can still return a valid result for the wrong question.

​You face this exact exposure when you deploy AI systems and automated compliance checks inside your business.

​An AI model can follow your prompt with high accuracy. An automated policy engine can pass 100% of its tests. Both systems still create legal and financial liability if the starting assumptions are flawed.

​Consider what happens when a flawed premise goes unchecked:

​- Your team builds an automated privacy filter using an outdated definition of personal data, and sensitive customer records leak into a third-party model.

​- Your hiring tool passes every internal fairness test because the test measures an indirect trait instead of actual job performance.

- ​Your contract review agent flags standard clauses accurately, but it misses a new statutory requirement that nobody added to its rule set.

​To protect your organization as AI workflows scale, audit your starting inputs before you audit the final outputs. Verify your starting definitions, legal classifications, and risk thresholds before you automate enforcement. Review those premises whenever laws or business operations change.

​If you audit only the final output, you miss errors built into the system from the start.

Are you building a business, or have you simply created a job that you can never take a day off from?
I think this is one of the biggest challenges freelancers face when trying to become entrepreneurs.

When you start freelancing, everything depends on you.
You find the clients.
You negotiate the contracts.
You deliver the work.
You handle customer enquiries.
You collect the payments.
And as your business grows, you become increasingly busy.

But here is the problem.

If your business cannot operate without you, have you really built a business?
Traditionally, the next step would be to hire employees, delegate responsibilities, and build a team. However, this is often much harder than it sounds. Hiring involves financial commitments, management responsibilities, and competition for talented people.

You also have to learn something that many entrepreneurs find particularly difficult: trusting others to do work that you have always done yourself. This is where I believe AI fundamentally changes the entrepreneurial journey. Instead of treating AI as nothing more than a tool for writing emails or generating images, I think entrepreneurs should start treating it as a collaborative thinking partner. Ask it to challenge your business model. Let it question your pricing strategy. Use it to identify operational weaknesses, organise workflows, and automate repetitive tasks.

You can even ask AI to argue against your business decisions, helping you examine assumptions you might otherwise overlook. Of course, AI cannot replace human judgement, customer relationships, or accountability. But it can help a solo entrepreneur begin operating with the structure and discipline of a larger organisation.

That is a remarkable opportunity. You may no longer need to hire your first employee before you can begin delegating certain tasks. And you can invest the time you save in developing products, attracting customers, and building sustainable revenue.

The real transition from freelancer to entrepreneur is not about working harder.
It is about building systems that create value without requiring your personal involvement in every single task. AI may not build your business for you. But it could help you stop being the bottleneck that prevents your business from growing.

JOB SEARCH AI TOOLKIT | POST 3 OF 5
FIND COMPANIES THAT MAY BE HIRING
One job search strategy is to look beyond job postings and identify companies that are growing, expanding, or investing in new teams.
You can use AI to research these opportunities.
1. FIND 20 TARGET COMPANIES
Prompt:
"I'm a job seeker targeting [Job Title] positions in [Industry].
Here are three companies I'm interested in:
[Company 1]
[Company 2]
[Company 3]
Identify 20 similar companies in the same industry or related markets.
For each company, provide:
Company name
Industry and business focus
Headquarters or relevant hiring location
Why it may be a good target for my role
Official careers page
Prioritize companies relevant to my experience and career goals."
2. IDENTIFY HIRING SIGNALS
Prompt:
"Act as a job market research analyst.
Find companies in [Industry] that may expand hiring for [Target Role] in [Location].
Research the following signals from the past 90 days:
Recent funding rounds
New leadership appointments
Product launches or partnerships
Three or more recent job postings in the relevant function
Multiple recent hires
New enterprise customers or major contracts
Prioritize companies showing multiple signals.
Classify each company:
LOW: 1 verified signal
MEDIUM: 2 verified signals
HIGH: 3 or more verified signals
Return a table with:
Company | Location | Hiring Signals & Dates | Signal Strength | Source Links | Why It May Suggest Hiring
Use reliable, recent sources. Clearly distinguish confirmed job openings from possible future hiring. Do not invent information or links."
3. PRIORITIZE YOUR TARGET LIST
Prompt:
"Based on the research above, rank the companies by relevance to my experience, target role, location, and verified hiring signals.
Recommend the top 10 companies I should research further and explain why."
MY TIP
Don't focus only on the number of jobs you apply for. Spend time identifying employers where your experience matches their current business needs.
Hiring signals are clues, not guarantees.

$2 million to $10 million a year saved by replacing outsourced customer service and document processing.

30% less spent on outside agencies for creative and content work.

$1 million a year saved on outsourced risk checks.

And these gains came without major workforce cuts.
The myth: "AI saves money by replacing your people."
The truth: In this research, the savings came from replacing work you already pay someone else to do.

That matters a lot in healthcare. Healthcare executives in the report did not expect to cut physician or clinical hiring over the next five years.

So where is the outside spend in a health system? Look here.

1. Outsourced coding and billing.
If you pay a vendor per chart, AI-assisted coding review can bring some of that work back in-house.

2. Outsourced call centers.
Appointment reminders and basic patient questions are often handled by a contracted team.

3. Transcription and document services.
Many groups still pay per line or per page.

4. Agencies and consultants.
Patient education materials, internal newsletters, and recruitment content.

Start by pulling your purchased services list. Every contract on it is a question: could AI help us do part of this ourselves?

Most leaders look for AI savings in the org chart. The ones who find them look in the vendor contracts.

How many qualified candidates never get the opportunity to have a conversation?
I have sat on both sides of the hiring table—as a candidate seeking an opportunity and as an operations leader responsible for staffing, budgets, service delivery, and retention.
With more than 20 years of management, director-level leadership, and hands-on experience, I believe we need to restore the human connection in hiring.
Applicant tracking systems and AI-assisted tools have a place. But when screening criteria become too rigid, do we risk overlooking people who can do the work simply because their résumés do not match a template?
A degree has value. So does experience managing P&Ls, protecting margins, negotiating contracts, developing teams, handling HR matters, and mitigating risk. Different paths can build strong leaders.
Following up on an application should not feel impossible.
I have contacted local branches only to reach someone unfamiliar with the opening. They direct me to corporate, and corporate refers me back to the branch. A generic rejection while the position remains advertised adds to the uncertainty.
Who owns the candidate experience?
I have also seen hiring decisions made outside the local market without enough input from those who understand its workforce, compensation expectations, and operational realities.
That connects directly to retention.
We often compete for the same local talent while operating within tight contract margins. But if winning business requires wages that make recruiting and retention difficult, we need to examine the full cost—not just the initial labor rate.
An additional $0.50 or $1.00 an hour can matter to someone balancing everyday expenses. So can recognition, respect, and opportunities to grow.
Before questioning employee loyalty, we should ask whether we are giving people a reason to stay.
What can we improve?
Separate essential qualifications from preferences, recognizing equivalent experience where appropriate.
Keep meaningful human review involved and use conversations or role-relevant assessments to evaluate capability beyond keywords.
Publish realistic pay ranges, schedules, and job expectations upfront.
Give applicants a clear contact, an expected timeline, and updates when a role is filled, paused, or canceled.
Align local branches, recruiters, and hiring managers—and include local leaders in compensation decisions.
Build realistic labor costs into bids, accounting for turnover, training, overtime, and service disruption.
Candidates are not asking employers to lower their standards. We are asking for a fair opportunity to demonstrate how we meet them.
A stronger candidate pool starts with a stronger hiring process. Retention starts with what happens next.
Recruiters, hiring managers, and operations leaders: What is one practical change you would make?

An AI hiring tool can be “advisory” in the contract—and decisive in practice.

On 11 November, the European Data Protection Board announced that its 2027 coordinated enforcement action will focus on automated decision-making, including AI-driven candidate screening, in recruitment.

This is an enforcement priority under existing GDPR rights, not a new prohibition on recruitment AI or a finding against any particular provider.

For in-house teams, the useful question is not simply whether a human appears somewhere in the workflow. It is whether that person can meaningfully assess and change the outcome.

A practical review should trace one candidate through the process:

* Can a score automatically remove them from consideration?
* Does the reviewer see the underlying information, or only a recommendation?
* Can the reviewer challenge the output—and are they equipped to do so?
* Can the organisation explain the process and respond to an access request?
* Does the supplier provide the information needed to answer those questions?

These are joint responsibilities for HR, privacy, procurement and technology teams.

For global organisations, a centrally purchased tool should not obscure local accountability. The strongest preparation is evidence of how decisions actually happen—not merely a policy saying that humans remain in control.

Bringing someone onto your team involves far more than agreeing on a salary—and the legal stakes of early onboarding mistakes have risen sharply.

According to 2026 research from the Economic Policy Institute, 10% to 30% of employers misclassify at least one worker as an independent contractor, and at least 12 states passed or introduced stricter misclassification laws across 2025–2026.

I've been thinking about how AI might affect the Indian IT industry, and I have a slightly different point of view.

I feel small and mid-sized IT companies could face the impact much sooner than giants like TCS, Infosys, Wipro and Accenture.

Think about a small business owner who needs a website, SEO, social media management, content, designs and lead generation.

Earlier, they would have to approach different agencies or hire people to get all this done.

Today, with AI tools, a small team can handle a lot of this work. Even business owners can do things they would have outsourced earlier.

Naturally, this could affect small agencies. Some clients may reduce their spending, while others may simply stop outsourcing certain services.

But when I think about companies like TCS, Infosys, Wipro and Accenture, I see a different situation.

These companies work with some of the world's biggest businesses. Their work involves systems that have been running for years, multiple departments, approvals, security requirements and long-term contracts.

Changing all of that isn't as simple as introducing a new AI tool.

That's why I think large IT companies might have more time to adapt.

However, there's another side to this.

A large part of the IT services business has traditionally depended on the number of people working on a project.

If AI allows 50 people to do work that previously required 100, what happens to the other 50?

The company may continue getting projects and generating revenue, but its hiring requirements could change.

I don't think TCS, Infosys or Accenture are going anywhere. But I do think the way they operate could look very different in the coming years.

My bigger concern is for the thousands of small and mid-sized IT companies that depend on traditional services and don't have the resources or time to change their business models quickly.

Maybe AI won't eliminate the IT industry. Maybe it will simply change who does the work, how much it costs and how many people are needed to do it.

Just a thought I've been exploring.

Do you think small IT companies will feel the impact first, while the bigger players get more time to adapt?

"Anything" is not a job description.

After church today, a small group of young women asked me for a job. When I asked what kind, they said: "anything." We have no openings, and when we do, a backlog of applications is waiting. I won't hire on the basis of a shared pew and call it youth empowerment. So I told them the honest thing: anyone can offer "anything", so nobody pays for it. Offer something worth something to the person you're asking.

I talked it over with my own kids afterwards: why people get paid at all. It left me with three views of the same problem.

1. Society: the bottom rung is going.

The first job used to be simple work: data capture, filing, typing, answering the phone, first drafts. That is exactly the work AI now does well and cheaply. Senior roles are safe for now. The entry rung is what disappears first, and everyone has to start on the entry rung. For a country as young as Zambia, that is a serious problem.

2. The young person: what is there to offer?

Education is necessary, and it is no longer enough. A certificate says you sat in class. An employer wants to know what you can do for them on Monday.

But what could those girls actually offer? Honestly, I don't know. Young men sell their strength, pushing wheelbarrows and carrying sacks of maize. Those are not desirable jobs, and for young women even that door is mostly shut. Many dream of nursing or teaching, a safe government job. About 570,000 young Zambians turn 18 each year. The government has hired about 42,000 teachers since 2022. The arithmetic leaves most of them outside.

3. The employer: every hire is a long commitment.

I use AI every day in my own business, so I see this side clearly. A hire costs far more than the salary: pension and health contributions, leave, gratuity, contracts, compliance, and the risk of a dispute that runs for months.

That burden is growing. A new minimum wage is being discussed. This week the Minister of Labour told employers that the minimum wage is "just a benchmark" and that they should pay "way better". He also said short contracts, the kind a pump attendant starts on, must carry gratuity and retirement benefits. Each step on its own sounds fair. Together they push one way: hiring a person gets more expensive, while automating gets cheaper and better.

I sympathise with the idea. Workers deserve fair pay, and deducting statutory contributions without remitting them is theft. But think of the pump attendant's job. Make it carry more and it gets better for whoever holds it. There will also be fewer of them. An employer facing a dearer hire doesn't hire more; they ask whether the job is needed at all. With automation as the alternative, the answer is "no" more often every year.

Our economy already fails to create enough jobs. And we are making people more expensive to hire just as machines become the better deal.

I don't have an answer. What would you have told them?

Move from administrative HR to a function that supports the company's mission, values and long-term goals. The course treats strategy as a cycle: assess where you are, forecast what you'll need, then build the plan.

What it covers
- Foundations: what strategic HR means, the competencies of strategic HR professionals, tying HR to the organization's mission and values, and getting HR a real presence with leadership
- Planning: when to run audits and assessments, how to build an HR strategic plan, and how AI can support it
- Applying strategy across the employee lifecycle: recruiting and onboarding, performance management, learning and growth, employee experience and culture, hybrid and contract workers, DIBs, and well-being and flexible work
- Execution: software, apps and metrics to measure the strategy, and strategic use of benefits and compensation

Why it's worth your time
It gives you one structure to organize everything HR already does, so each program (hiring, training, pay, culture) answers to the same business goals. If you're in a small HR team where everything feels urgent, that structure is what lets you decide what to do first and what to say no to.

Things you should (and should not do) as a finance leader in your first 100 days somewhere new:

1. Find the cash. All of it.

How much is there, where is it, and who controls it? Seriously, who has the bank logins? Do they still work here? You might find accounts nobody has touched in years.

2. Build a 13-week cash flow forecast.

You could end the month with $5M in the bank without realizing you dipped below $1M two weeks earlier. Forecast receipts and payments weekly.

This advice came from Keith Durden , who’s been the new guy 5x at VC and PE-backed companies.

3. Challenge inherited working capital terms.

At PartsTech, I changed supplier terms from net 45 to net 30. People said suppliers would revolt. Only two of the top ten pushed back. We’d been giving away 15 days because that’s how it had always been done.

4. Find the people who know where the bodies are buried.

Not necessarily the senior people. Find those who remember why decisions were made. The org chart doesn’t tell you where all the influence sits.

5. Give your accounting team a couple of closes before passing judgment.

Do they meet deadlines? Are the numbers right? Can they explain reconciliations with actual transactions? Do they bring you opinions on what to do next?

6. Follow a dollar through the business.

Have your CRO and CMO walk you through one real customer: acquisition channel, cost, contract, revenue recognition, cash collection. You’ll learn things the P&L doesn’t tell you.

7. Understand fixed, variable, and step-function costs.

At Worth AI , Keith explained the company could spend $1M on data whether revenue is $0 or $30M. Extrapolating historical gross margins misses the operating leverage.

8. Build retention reporting you trust.

Especially cohorted NRR. Who’s expanding, contracting, churning, and why? If the reporting doesn’t exist, put it on your roadmap.

9. Don’t confuse changing things with improving things.

You don’t need a new ERP or chart of accounts in month one. A temporary reporting layer might get you 90% of the way without disruption. Is the change for your comfort or the business’s benefit?

10. Operate like the company could be sold tomorrow.

Document EBITDA add-backs as they happen. Clean up historical financials. Keep the support and rationale for your decisions.

In a PE-backed business, you’re always potentially for sale.

One last thing: By day 100, you should have a view on the people, systems, cash, and economics. You don’t have to have fixed them all.

There’s pressure to prove hiring you was a good idea. Sometimes that means understanding what you inherited before rearranging the furniture.

Another AI movie—hear me out before you scroll past.

Making a film has always been a dream of mine, even when the obstacles felt huge: budget, tech, and needing hundreds of talented artists to pull it off. Lately, with short contracts, outsourcing, and tough hiring cycles, it’s been harder than ever for an average artist trying to keep a foothold in the industry.

The good news is that the barrier to entry is shifting. If you have a budget, tools like Higgsfield and OpenArt can help you push 4K visuals, consistent characters, and cinematic shots. When you don't have the budget—like me—you find another way.

Over the past two months, I leaned on open-source and free tools like ComfyUI, Blender, and ArtCraft to build a scrappy pipeline from scratch. Story, script, storyboards, character and environment design, sound, and editing—all on a $0 budget. It wasn't always smooth. There were plenty of sleepless nights, roadblocks, and technical headaches, and it’s definitely not perfect yet. Still, with existing 3D/art skills and patience, a small team—or even one person—can get surprisingly close to something presentable and entertaining.
